outputs.final_proof:
\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be a linearly ordered set with its order topology. We use the following interval lemma.

\emph{Interval lemma.} If $x$ belongs to a basic open set $B$ of the order topology, then there is an open set $V$ with $x\in V$ and $\overline V\subseteq B$.

To prove the lemma, suppose first that $B=(a,b)$. If points can be chosen on both sides of $x$ inside $B$, choose $a<c<x<d<b$ and set $V=(c,d)$. Since $\overline{(c,d)}\subseteq[c,d]$, we obtain $\overline V\subseteq[c,d]\subseteq(a,b)$. If one side has no available interior point, then $x$ is adjacent to the corresponding endpoint, and the appropriate one-sided basic neighborhood, such as $(a,x]$ or $[x,b)$, has closure contained in $[a,x]$ or $[x,b]$ and hence in $B$; if both sides are unavailable, $B=\{x\}$ and $V=\{x\}$. For a basic ray, use the same argument on its finite side. This proves the lemma.

Now let $U$ be any open neighborhood of $x$. Choose a basic open set $B$ with $x\in B\subseteq U$. The lemma gives an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ such that
\[
x\in V\subseteq\overline V\subseteq B\subseteq U.
\]
Thus $X$ is regular. (It is also $T_1$, because each singleton is closed: its complement is open.)
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be a linearly ordered set with the order topology. We verify the regularity criterion directly: for every $x\in U$ with $U$ open, there is an open $V$ such that $x\in V\subseteq\overline V\subseteq U$.

Choose a basic neighborhood $B$ of $x$ with $B\subseteq U$. If $B$ is an open interval $(a,b)$, choose a smaller interval around $x$ whenever possible. If there are $c,d$ with $a<c<x<d<b$, let $V=(c,d)$; then
\[
\overline V\subseteq[c,d]\subseteq(a,b)=B.
\]
If $x$ is adjacent to $a$ or $b$, use the corresponding one-sided basic neighborhood; its closure is contained in the closed interval between $x$ and the chosen interior point, which lies in $(a,b)$. If $x$ is adjacent to both endpoints, then $B=\{x\}$, which is open and closed. If $B$ is a basic ray at a minimum or maximum, apply the same construction on its only finite side; if that side has no interior point, the ray is a singleton. Thus in every case there is an open $V$ with
\[
x\in V\quad\text{and}\quad\overline V\subseteq B\subseteq U.
\]

Finally, $X$ is $T_1$ because the complement of each singleton is a union of open intervals and rays. Therefore $X$ is regular.
\end{proof}
